cells.tense: Something you've kept alive is arriving at your door now, and you're the one meeting it.
cells.ask: Offer to pass one thing you know to one person in your own words today, then stop and let it be theirs — the passing is what they get.
cells.core:
Something you carry from before has arrived at your door, and you're the one meeting it. You've kept a thing alive across people and years — a way of doing a meal, a phrase, a reason to show up — and it's still breathing because you've adjusted it while keeping what mattered. You can belong to something and still not disappear into it. That's the good version. You don't need to defend it or sell it.

What's arriving now is small and ordinary: a moment where the meaning could pass to someone else. If you meet it, you hand one piece on — not the whole inheritance, one piece, in words that sound like you. Then you let it go. The tuning is the work; the balance costs one uneven attempt where you can't control how it lands.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something alive and passing it on your own terms.
cells.verb: carrying meaning between people, making it common
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving enters and is met

cells.tense: You're bracing for a version of this where the people around you finally keep it the way you keep it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been insisting on and go without it today. Say nothing about why; let the version without it stand.
cells.core:
You're already living a few steps ahead. Out in front is a room where the people near you finally do it the right way, keep it the right way, agree it's the only right way — and the next conversation keeps getting steered toward that room. So the thing that was supposed to hold people together is becoming a test they keep failing. The tradition is breathing less and the rulekeeping is doing the talking.

What's arriving is a moment where a window could stay open. You've sealed a few yourself. There's another move here, one that isn't loosening everything: let one false structure fall that was only ever held up by your grip. Let the next version, whatever it turns out to be, get through the frame you built.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding so tight the thing can't breathe.
cells.verb: carrying meaning between people, making it common

cells.tense: The door is behind you — you went through it alone, and you haven't looked back.
cells.ask: Ask one person what they do over and over in their own life, then tell them what you see — one plain sentence, today.
cells.core:
Nothing has arrived for a while, and you've stopped expecting it. You build your own version of everything from scratch — your own ways of marking time, your own reasons, your own company — and each one works for about a season. Then it's back to the drawing board. That isn't failing; it's a lot of engine with no road. What's missing is a framework, something bigger than the day you're in, passed down or passed over, that you could belong to without shrinking.

That's not nostalgia. Seeing the pattern comes before picking a place in it. Other people have patterns too. Watch one, and say out loud what you noticed — one sentence, plainly, while it's still fresh.
cells.sheetLine: You keep starting from zero and building the same thing.
cells.verb: carrying meaning between people, making it common
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving enters and is met

cells.tense: You're already passing something to the people around you — they take it in — and you'd say you were just being yourself.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person that something you do is yours to hand on, once, in plain words — no explaining it after.
cells.core:
Something is being passed on already, and you're the one passing it. You do things your own way and the people around you copy them, or ask why you do them that way, and you answer as if it were all just habit. It isn't. You keep a small piece of the world's meaning alive in the people within reach — a way of treating a stranger, a phrase your family says, a reason to sit down together. They're learning it from you right now.

The signal is bigger than the credit you take. Owning it doesn't inflate you — it tunes you. When you say plainly that something is yours to carry and hand on, you can adjust it on purpose instead of by accident. The adjustment is the whole of it: a steady hand on what passes through.
cells.sheetLine: You're already teaching it. You just haven't claimed it.
